text: Welcome. Recording in progress. I'd like to call together our special session on legislative priorities with our legislators on December 1st here at 10 a.m. room 241. We've got Supervisor Ann Malick of the Whitehall District, Supervisor Michael Pruitt of the Scottsdale District, Supervisor D'Anthony Kim of the Jack Jewel District, Supervisor B. Lepisto-Kirtley of the Nevada District, Supervisor Ned Galloway of the Rio District, Myself, Jim Andrews, representing the Samuel Miller District.

So we have a course and are ready to go on. Also, I want to call attention to all of your welcomes. I'm Mr. Richardson, Jeff Richardson, our county executive. Mr. Andy Herrick, our county attorney. The Assembly Kilroy, director of economic development at the table.

Kevin Dermott, deputy director of planning behind. I'll mention David Plump, who is in the audience of the Thomas Jefferson Planning District Commission. I'll also like to welcome our Head of Police Officers, President Officer Enzo Irizarry and Officer Lauren Dayling.
Thank you for your service today and everything on our behalf. But mostly, I really want to welcome our, well, at this point, our Delegate President, Amy Lawford of the 55th House District.

Welcome, Delegate Lawford. I'm honored to have you here, and I look forward to the conversation about our breweries. I hope we'll be joined soon by a delegate. Yes, she is. On our way. She says she'll be here. Tina Colson, 54th House District.

And we're also joined, thank you, Tracy Eckert, Legislative Director for Senator Greta-Bades. We're unable to be here today, but you'll be representing him, and we appreciate your presence. Thank you. I would love to give all the background and all the honors, but I think we want to get right to it because two hours goes very quickly.
And I'm going to turn it over, if that's okay, to Emily Kilroy, who's first going to open with some description of her future's project and AstraZeneca. Excellent. Thank you, Supervisor Andrews.

Thank you to the whole Board of Supervisors. I forget to mention Claudette Forkerson, our clerk, For our legislators and the Board of Supervisors, thank you for the time this morning. This is the rough look at the agenda, and I'm going to transition to the podium.

Andy Herrick, the county attorney, and Kevin McDermott and I will take us through some slides, and then there's plenty of time for discussion throughout. If you have a burning question about anything that we're going over, please feel free to ask a question. Don't feel like you need to wait. And I'm excited to be talking about AstraZeneca and really an update on the Rodana Futures Project in the context of the AstraZeneca announcement earlier this year.

And we wanted to take a minute as part of the legislative forum to go over some of this with you all. Many of you were able to join us at the announcement event itself, and you've certainly seen some of the news articles. But we wanted to sort of recognize the support that we've had at the state level on the Rodana Futures project, which has been many years in the making, but really positioned us to be successful for AstraZeneca, and we thought it was important to just recognize that a little bit today.

So this is a graphic from the Ravanna Futures work that we've really kicked off in earnest in 2023 that you all have seen before. It sort of lays out the context for the county's land acquisition directly adjacent to Ravanna Station, which is a military installation in Alcumarro County that is the operating location for the National Ground Intelligence Center.

There's a Defense Intelligence Agency presence here and support teams from the National Geospatial Intelligence Agency, and that's in the areas labeled number one, two, and three. There's a private office building that is located directly adjacent to the secure perimeter there. That is office space that's used by the mission of Ravana Station. And then there had been, for a very long time, all of this undeveloped property around Ravana Station.

And several years ago, the county got really in partnership with the state, the Veterans of Defense Affairs Secretariat, a real focus on this being the only military installation in the Commonwealth of Virginia that has land available for expansion surrounding it. So every other location in the Commonwealth is either surrounded by development or surrounded by water. And the defense sector is a really critically important one for the Virginia economy. And so it was of keen interest, really driven out of that office.

We talked last time we were together about this idea that the Robana Futures Project was locally driven, state supported and federally shared. So much bigger of an opportunity than just Albemarle County. And there's a lot of things to say about that now. So state-supported staff have been invited to participate in annual briefings to the GAMVIC.

Many of you have joined us at those briefings over the years just to give sort of a state of the property and the mission set there. Compared to other military installations in the Commonwealth, Rhode Island Station has flown a little bit below the radar because of the nature of the work that they do there. And so it's been really important to sort of raise awareness through those General Assembly Military Veterans Caucus meetings about the work that they do here in Albemarle.

You all have been very supportive with state budget requests introduced in 2024 and 2025 towards providing a future site readiness. And while state budget requests have not been successful through the end of the process, We think a lot of that has raised a lot of awareness about the opportunity, and we have been successful in getting $11 million in site readiness funding from the state, from the entities listed there, which have really enabled us to advance the work for property development that, again, has positioned us really well for the AstraZeneca opportunity.

So I just really wanted to take a moment to say thank you for the support at the state level in helping to bring this vision that has felt multi-decade to fruition so quickly. And so this is an update to that graphic.

This is showing where AstraZeneca will be located as they complete their development over the next several years. It's a total of 82 acres of the property, which is incredible. The earlier version of this graphic had this area labeled as 30 acres.

and this was a combined 55 acres through the process of working with AstraZeneca to site your facility we've sort of re-looked at how we conceived what areas are developable and what areas are not developable we had originally conceived this area in particular as being perhaps office suited for office type uses manufacturing footprint is much different than office and so we've learned a lot along the way on what's possible.

And so you'll see that the total developable acreage has increased significantly, and we'll be focusing on making sure that AstraZeneca lands successfully on the timeline that they have identified for their facility to open, as well as what the future for this Land Bay 25 and this now Land Bay 55 look like, and that's some of the exciting work ahead.

This is a concept, early concept, for what the after Zeneca facility will look like this is the office building that will be sort of the front door to the facility there's a lot of green building principles sort of hidden in this picture there's laminated timber construction lots of opportunities for daylighting they have a real strong corporate commitment to sustainable building practices and we look forward as they refine their designs to being able to share more what that looks like like, but really living the value of sustainability through their built environment.

Just some of the numbers that we're excited about. It's one biopharmaceutical manufacturing campus. They're actually locating two manufacturing facilities within that. It sits on 82 acres. There'll be 600 direct new jobs associated with the facilities, primarily manufacturing jobs, but as you might imagine, HR finance type functions will be located there as well.

They're estimating 3,000 construction jobs that will last several years to build a facility and prep the land for it. And then AstraZeneca, from their own experience in other places, has a multiplier of every job they create directly. It indirectly creates five jobs, and so their number is 3,000 indirect and induced jobs associated with what they do there.

The minimum salary for these jobs is $125,000 a year, which is just incredible, especially given that so many are manufacturing jobs. And the capital investment by the company on the property will be $4.5 billion. I talked a little bit about green building.

They do have a corporate commitment to carbon-neutral operations in the next several years. And so they'll be working on-site to site solar panels on top of roofs, some ground solar panels as well, And then any additional energy that they need to power the facility, they're working with their energy provider to get green energy out of their production portfolio.

And then they also have a big emphasis on closing systems as part of their manufacturing process. We highlight this information because one of the first cuts that they made when they were looking for a facility in Virginia was communities that have a commitment to sustainability, and Albemarle County made it through that cut very strongly because of some of the work that the Board of Supervisors has led on climate action, biodiversity action, etc. The two facilities have two different production types. One is a biologics facility, the other is small molecules.

You can see just a little bit of information about when they plan to open and the types of buildings that will be associated with each. And that's what I have on that. Again, really just wanted to make sure that you all have the latest information on the AstraZeneca project. Thank you again for your continued support. And with that, I'm going to introduce Kevin McDermott to talk about transportation. Hello, I'm Kevin McDermott. I'm the Deputy Director of Planning here at Almar County. And I was asked to talk a little bit about

transportation funding in Almar County. As I get started, I just want to make sure that everyone recognizes that Almar County, like most localities and state, primarily relies on state funding to do our transportation projects, and we do that through two major programs. Smart Scale, which I'm going to really focus on in this presentation, and then the revenue sharing program.

I don't have a lot on that because it's a fairly stable program. It provides every other year $10 million that would be matched with a local amount of $10 million for any transportation project that we select. That is we've made right now about $200 million available in the state overall for those programs.

That has not really kept up with inflation. $200 million does go far, though, and so we've taken advantage of that almost every year. We really do come close to maximizing that $10 million in state funding by matching with the local match.

But I'm going to focus more in this presentation on smart scale because really that's where we get the significant amount of funding that we rely on for our transportation projects. All the major projects will come out of that program. So this is some information that came from our Culpeper District Planning Department.

And what you can see here is each round of SmartScale. So six rounds we've had. And just to remind everybody that in the first two rounds, those were annual, and then they went to biannually after that. So really, if you wanted to compare apples to apples, then you would want to add those two, round one and round two together.

And really, I want to focus on a few of these numbers. What you can see here is the total funding. This is statewide what has been requested. And you can see that that number has remained generally similar with a little bit of an increase towards the end here.

And then, of course, the total funding allocated. And once again, you see that number. It was high in those first couple years and remained generally the same through these last three years with a little bit of a decrease recently.

And the important thing to note about that is that when you look at the number of projects that were funded throughout the state, You can see that number has kind of gone down, and this most recent round, the round that was awarded in the FY26 six-year plan, was only 53 projects in the entire state.

So throughout all of Virginia, only 53 projects were awarded money through SmartScale, this primary source of funds that we have for transportation. Moving down a little more locally, Culpeper SmartScale allocations.

This just shows the way SmartScale is done is it's broken up into two different pots of money. One is for the high-priority projects, and the second is for the district grant program. So the district grant program for us only comes from, we only compete against the Culpeper district projects.

And what you can see here, once again, is that the numbers have gone up and down throughout the years, But the number of projects that got funded in Culpeper, you know, remained fairly steady if you were to average those.

But once again, in this most recent round, you see that dropping down to only four projects in the entire Culpeper district, which is very few. We did get one of those awards. Kevin, do you want us to ask questions at the end? Or do you want us to... What do you want to do? Any preference?

Okay, great. I was going to say, while you're mentioning both of those slides, can you help us with the why? Yes, and I'm actually going to kind of move into that. Okay, that's good. I just think that's an important question. Yeah, and I will say that the Commonwealth Transportation Board is the one who identifies the funding.

They're given an amount of funding for transportation overall. First, they pull out the maintenance funds, and one of the reasons we've seen these numbers go down is because maintenance costs have gone up, and so that maintenance comes out first, and then they divide all the other money up among all the different construction programs they have.

And one of those is the Smart Scale Program, so the High Priority Project Industry Grant Program. So that's why some of those numbers have gone down a little bit. And so this is Albemarle County. This is how we have done over these past six rounds. The orange are the projects that we did not get funded.

The blue are the projects that were funded. So you can see, you know, we've, when we're allowed to put in four applications from Alamara County, but also the Charlottesville-Alamara MPO is allowed to put in four additional ones, and the Thomas Jefferson Planning District Commission is also allowed to put in four.

We continuously go to them and say, hey, if you have extra room for applications, could we get some more applications submitted on our behalf? And that's why you see that we have been consistently asking, putting in about 12 applications every year.

More recently, we were instructed that we should really focus on higher priority projects for the county and for the state through their VTRANS programs, things that were identified through VTRANS. And so we have reduced that number a little bit.

We only did eight in this most recent round. But what you can see there is that we had a good year in round four there. In round four, the county did actually put in some of our local funds to try and buy down the cost of those projects.

This is a cost-benefit scoring analysis that's done. And so that allowed us to get quite a few projects. We put in about $9 million of local funds in that year. Other than that, though, we've remained kind of steady. And we've had these couple years, including this most recent one, where you only have one project funded.

This just gives you kind of an idea as to what's going on there. So this is the total amount that Albemarle County has requested for each round. And in round three, I'll just say the reason that spike is there is because we actually submitted three projects for the Hydraulic 29 interchange.

I'm sure you all know that's a really big, important interchange. There were three different proposals for that, and so that's why that number jumped up. Each one was almost $100 billion. But when you look at the median amount of all those projects that were requested, you can see that it still remained even until you get in these last couple years.

And that sort of gets to your question, Supervisor McKeel, is that what we've seen is that the cost of projects is significantly increased in these past two rounds, That huge jump you see in the median that we've requested is kind of indicative of that.

And then just to give one example of this, this is a recent project that we had submitted. We submitted it, the actual cost estimate was done in 2022. This was two rounds ago. And it's for a roundabout proposal out on 250 right in front of Western Albemarle.

I don't know if you all know where that is. This is Old Trail, and so you can see it was a pretty standard roundabout. You may have two lanes in most directions with one lane here. That cost estimate in 2022 was almost $13 million.

In 2024, it was unsuccessful. When we submitted it, it went up 30%, and the only difference you can see in that is that we moved a stormwater basin from property that the county didn't own to property that the county did own.

So that was intended to try and reduce the cost of this. So it just is kind of an example of how we see costs increasing. And so I think overall what we're looking at here is that although monies remain steady and we're really grateful for the wins that we've had, the cost of all the projects has continuously gone up.

And so that's really where we're struggling to try and get all of our priority projects implemented. And I'll also say that just down the road from here, you all have probably gone through the 151-250 roundabout that was constructed quite a few years ago now.

That was submitted in around, I think the cost estimate was done in 2016. That roundabout, very similar to this one, was only $5.8 million. So that gives another idea as to how that cost increases occurred. Matt, I'm going to pass it on to you here.

Yeah, I think at this point we're going to take a moment and see if there are any additional comments. And I'm going to go through, starting with Supervisor Calloway, any comments on the transportation aspect? Is that a kind of simple discussion? I don't have any comments on the Ravenna Futures.

The transportation funding discussion, I think I'll make a couple additional points. One, just a few weeks ago at Vaco, and now for two years in a row, it doesn't really matter the size of the county. whether it's rural or urban, whether it's northern Virginia or southwest, everybody's talking about transportation funding, not just the funding of it, but then also the criteria to get things approved. And it's a problem across the board.

So it's not just Albemarle County. I think when you have over, in the last round of SmartScale, over $30 billion in applications made when jurisdictions have to limit their applications. So if you only get four and it changed the last round what the MPOs and the PDCs can submit.

So the criteria of what they could submit, like Kevin talked about in years past, we've maxed what we can ask through them. Can't do it that way anymore because now they can only submit certain types of projects, so now you can't even get your full 12 applications in, right? So, you know, these aren't fluff projects.

They're safety priorities. They're economic development priorities. their congestion and flow priorities that match what the state says they want these transportation projects to be. But at the end of the day, in Albemarle County, how many things are on our transportation priorities list? 165.

165 transportation priorities, and we can submit four every two years through SmartSkill. So, you know, we just had Thanksgiving, and I've noticed something at my house. When I host a dinner for 10 people, if six more want to show up, I either have to carve up the portions even further for them, or I have to go get more portions.

Or I'm going to be a bad host because their pie is a lot thinner than what it was the year before. VDOT just told us at an MPO meeting last month that this next round of SmartScale is going to be even more competitive than the current round, and Albemarle didn't receive any applications that we submitted other than one that was portioned to Pantops that was already in play and had gone through a couple of rounds before.

And they're not very big additions. But I think the only reason they got approved is because with the DDI and the other things they've been doing on Pantops, if you don't do these, then you limit what the impact of that project does. So all this is to say whether it's rural roads, whether it's secondary roads, whether it's smart scale, you have maintenance costs that are rising, and you have transportation projects throughout the whole commonwealth that need to be done that aren't fluff.

And there's clearly not enough resources to get them done. And it becomes the question of what can you do about that? Delegate Reed this year at Vaco sounded like he was talking off of the same talking points that Delegate Austin spoke about the year before at Vaco.

And when I hear a Republican say the same things as a Democrat and they don't really answer the question about what they're going to do about transportation funding. They explain why we're in the funding system. They seem to understand why we are where we are. But I don't ever hear any possible solutions of how we're going to fix it other than, well, we've been thinking about trying to figure out if mileage used could be done and how we could do it.

But people don't want dongles in their cars. Well, that's to me just not, with all due respect, because I've never discussed this with you all, but that's really not a real educated conversation to have when we're barely funding a limited application request for one program, a third of projects that required a billion dollars of local matches.

So I've been talking to my colleagues at the TJPDC. You all should have received a letter. I don't know if you had a chance to read it about a month or so ago where all the counties that are under the TJPVC footprint agreed and spoke to the need and the situation that is transportation funding.

And we hope that you all will take this seriously going into this round. I know there's a lot of competing things. You are working at a scale that, you know, we all have similar things that we work with. The hard one about transportation, is this something our citizens come to with this all the time? And I can't just say, well, we could raise your taxes, I guess, here in Albemarle, because that won't do anything about transportation funding, because it's dictated through the state. So I'm hoping you all can speak to that today. And I don't, you know, I understand where it's at. Delegate Reed did a good job of explaining what some of the big concerns are for the state budget. But at the end of the day, it's not an R or

a D issue. This is an issue where these projects aren't going to get less. Maintenance isn't going to go down, costs aren't going to go down. It's my opinion that we have to find a way to increase the portions and figure out what we're going to do about transportation funding or else the state's really going to languish with unmaintained roads, poorly operating roads, and no way to improve situations that are now critically a problem. So I appreciate you giving me a chance to speak my mind on it.

Thank you, and I want to make sure that we recognize those relevant remarks and just add on, but we need to add on from there. So, Supervisor, please talk her. I agree with everything that Supervisor Galloway said. I just wanted to ask you said that there's a pot of money that comes from the state. Some of it goes for what the counties asked for and the others, the other monies go for I think it was I mean, there's a lot of different programs Yeah, just to fix the roads. Yeah, so there's a maintenance fund and then really the construction fund

and the construction fund's broken up in multiple different... Right. So the maintenance fund, I think that hasn't gone up either, right? I believe that has increased, yes. And that's what goes to VDOT to maintain our roads and then cities get apportioned out by their mile.

And so that's my concern also, is that We also have these, I get calls a lot that VDOT is not maintaining the road or VDOT is not filling the potholes and things like that, which that's important also.

I mean, not only the projects that we have that we would like funded, but also the maintenance of the roads. If that money's going down also, that's going to just increase, you know, dangerous roads. And I consider it a safety issue also, because that's what's happening, is that if we're not maintaining our roads, that is a safety issue.

So that's my input. Ms. McKenna. I think we all agree with what Ned said, and we said it very succinctly and clearly. I would just add that Alamo County, the last couple of years, to pipeline projects.

Pipeline projects declared by BIDAD, which means that they were projects of state significance. BIDAD intentionally delayed one of the pipeline projects, which was the Abbey Road or Abbey Road 250. They delayed that to come back and try to figure out a better solution, but the Barracks Road pipeline project that was It's not funded. None of it is funded.
So to add to what Ned said, you have VDOT declared pipeline projects that are really important transportation projects based on statewide significance, right, that are not being funded.

We've got to do something, folks. We've got to make the pie better. We used to say that when I was on the school board all the time. We take the pie and we cut it in different sections, but the pie has to get better. Thank you. I would just, again, endorse the points that Supervisor Galloway made.

And I would further add, it's not lost on me that the caucus is disproportionately represented by people who are serving incorporated cities. These issues do not fall in the same way, and communities that are served by comprehensive transit systems who might not have these issues land on them the same way.

This year we've seen growth in the caucus from communities that are not necessarily in incorporated cities, which I think might create a window of opportunity here. And I would further raise that, you know, delegate law firm specifically, you are kind of alone in representing a very rural, county-specific community heretofore.

And I would hope that this puts you in a really strong position to lead on this issue as someone who represents communities that are particularly impacted that has more security than this new tranche of people who would be joining than that. Thank you. Just two quick things to add regarding Marvanna Station.

Years and years of hard work went on behind the scenes, and timing is everything, as they say, so when the stars align, that was the reason why all of that was able to take that quantum leap forward. I don't think anybody snapped their fingers and this happened, and I just want to make sure people understand.

Transportation, in my opinion, is a Governor Willis moment here where he staked his entire reputation on a tax increase dedicated to massive transportation improvements and he did not get run out of office it was a wonderful success and until the recession came along in 2008 and took away 700 employees and massive amounts of funding which was never replaced since then we're back where we are and we have 3 million more people since he was governor So I understand, I agree with all the things that have been put forward, and it's a real

situation that the Assembly will have to face, but hopefully some strong leadership will happen and get some serious changes, not just pushing the chairs around long time. Thank you. And a couple of comments made by my colleagues on the board.

I'll add one comment, sort of on a left field, and I know that I've read that housing is an issue throughout the Commonwealth, and that there will be a certain amount of focus on housing. And, of course, when you have developed housing development projects in the county, we get a lot of feedback from residents.

And one of the things we hear most common from residents is that, oh, this is going to just ruin our transportation. Because every time we increase it, that's why we're adding more cars potentially on the road if we don't do it right. And we need that transportation to be functioning a little better than it has been.
So put that on there as well. Thank you. I can just say that I've gone on too many workshops about funding for, and a lot of things are happening.

I could probably just echo what Delegate Reed said, so I won't, but I know that this is an issue. And, you know, the way we fund transportation is through a fuel tax, but most of the cars are way more fuel efficient than they were when we started this.

And then compound that to the electric vehicles, which is part of why there is an electric vehicle tax, because we're trying to get money for the transportation. But it's something, and there's a lot of questions about what is the transparency for VDOT.

So I know I've been talking with Delegate Delaney, she's the chair of transportation, about what is this criteria. And there's a lot of ways we could be more efficient, which asphalt recycling, which is something I'm working on, making sure that we can make the road with the same asphalt and actually save millions of dollars, if not billions, and time efficiency.
So that's the kind of where I've been trying to focus my energy on, is how can we do it more efficiently and cost-effectively. But there is a discussion definitely going on right now. Thank you.

Amy, could I just add to what you were talking about, not efficiencies? The Highway Research Council a few years back used to report that suggested that bridges in Virginia wouldn't be washed to rid them of the salt.

And they said the life expectancy of the bridges would be expanded exponentially just to get the salt off of them. And what VDOT would have said was that they didn't have the money to wash the bridges. I'm just saying that some of those sorts of things, yes, and that's another example of what you're talking about.

I was just trying to give you another example. Thank you. Well, you know, I will definitely look into this. If it was in the packet, I would have like, you know, me, I would have dove head first. So I can get back to you with some of what the discussion has been from the chair of transportation.

Yeah, I would just, oh, Tracy, did you want to go? Tracy's like, no, good. I would echo what Supervisor Pruitt said, and I think there's a window of opportunity that's happening right now. Not to use fluff language, but we have a whole new administration coming in. So, you know, you're talking about frustrations you have felt over the past couple of years.

My hope is that conversations like this, this is new to me, Supervisor Galloway. I had not heard conversations about BDOT in our meetings in the past, so it's new to me. I hope conversations like this will make their way to Governor Spanberg and her team. There's going to be a brand new administration.

I'm presuming a lot of new people in the Department of Transportation. And it would absolutely, Supervisor Malik, be a time where there could be a moment to focus on transportation. So I would encourage you guys to continue to do the advocacy you're doing on it at the state level. And then I don't have, I mean, I will just be honest, I don't have much more to offer on the transportation.

I don't sit on the transportation committee. It's not typically my wheelhouse. I would have to get prepared. What I can offer you is that Amy and I sit on finance, and we did just do the finance retreat, and they gave us the predictions about what they're seeing next year, so I'm happy to share that with you all, the slides that we got about the transportation.

And then I can just tell you that the pie metaphor almost doesn't even work anymore. The pie is all kinds of messed up right now. We got federal things happening that are making the pie having to get split up in ways that don't even make sense. And so the work that I've done, and I know if Senator Deeds was here, would echo it has been so much on the Medicaid front. It is just such a big chunk of the pie that my conversations haven't really been on the transportation front. All that to say, I hear you, because it was loud and clear, and it was repeated by all of you, that VDOT is the frustration, and that your projects aren't getting funded, and that our roads are not being upkept the way that they need to be, and there needs to be something done. So thank you for bringing it.

It's not typically what I hear. And I would just mention, too, Highway 81 was a major project that was really siphoning in a lot of funds which is kind of closing we're in the closing stages of that so that was a major effort and that was multi-jurisdictions and that was really the rural aspect was to make that a safer highway and I know a lot of funds have been specific to that and then of course we were trying to extend rail up in northern Virginia into the Fredericksburg-Stafford counties so So, you know, I hear you.

I will also add finance is one area that I do actually anticipate there being a bit of movement. You're talking about taxes, finances, taxation, and how we give revenue for our state. And I do think there will be movement there. It's going to be the first time that there's been kind of an administrative change. There's going to be majorities in place.

There's things that can be done to kind of right-size the taxation in Virginia that could make it so that regular people are not necessarily being taxed more, but we are having more revenue generated, there's lots of options on the table. So I think it is actually an exciting year to talk about how to get different revenue in.

I think they said when I would be able to say, I wish Congress was here instead of Richmond. Thank you for carrying the message back. We'll turn it back over to Mr. Herrick, and we'll discuss our legislative program and legislative positions.
Good morning, I'm Andy Herrick, the county attorney. It's a pleasure to be with you all this morning. And I'm going to be going over in just a few brief slides the county's 2026 legislative program.

Before I begin presenting on that, in addition to Ms. Kilgore, I'd like to thank our legal services coordinator, James Douglas, and David Vaughn with the TJPDC for their work in preparing this year's program. What we did this year is we reorganized and restructured our program to hopefully make it more succinct and easier for folks to present and to discuss.

We replaced a series of nearly 50 legislative positions with a series of priorities and principles, and each of you should have on your desks in front of you the county's legislative program, and I'll walk again through very briefly in a few slides, the priorities, the principles, and then the positions as well.

So among the county's priorities, we have four basic priorities, three of which have to do with proposed amendments to the Virginia Code, and one of which is a proposed budget amendment. The first of the Code amendments is to enable localities to enforce the Virginia Landlord Tenant Act, and that is because what we're finding is that so many tenants find themselves in substandard housing, have issues, and don't have the resources to enforce it.
